questions.prompt: Architecture vs detailed design — architecture's distinctive focus is:
options: Non-functional / quality requirements (detailed design picks up the functional ones)
questions.explain: From the Ch1 design-process slide: **architecture answers the quality/non-functional questions** (performance, modifiability, security…); detailed design realizes the functional requirements within that skeleton.

questions.prompt: A module reads and MODIFIES another module's internal data directly. This is which (worst) coupling type?
questions.explain: **Content coupling** = relying on/modifying another module's INTERNALS — the most severe. **Common** = shared globals; **Data** = parameters only (the acceptable kind). Ranking worst→best: content > common > control > stamp > data.

questions.prompt: Coupling vs cohesion — good design means:
options: LOW coupling between modules + HIGH cohesion within each module
questions.explain: Coupling measures interdependence BETWEEN modules; cohesion measures how related tasks WITHIN one module are. They reinforce each other: a module focused on one well-defined task (high cohesion) needs fewer hooks into other modules' internals (low coupling). High coupling + low cohesion = changes ripple system-wide. Fix: re-modularize, hide internals behind stable interfaces, communicate via parameters only.

questions.prompt: Select THREE of the documented challenges of software design (from the slides):
options: Fast-changing technology that must co-exist with old tech
questions.explain: The slide's five challenges: **Requirements (volatility)** — 'a bigger house with more windows by next week'; **Technology (fast-changing)**; **Processes (inconsistency)**; **Ethics** (professional practice under pressure); **Management of design influences** (competing stakeholder concerns).

questions.prompt: UML diagram categories — which row is correct?
options: Structural = STATIC aspects (Class, Component) · Behavioral = DYNAMIC aspects (Use Case, Sequence)
Behavioral diagrams are deprecated in UML 2
questions.explain: **Structural** = static elements and interrelationships: Class, Component (also Object, Deployment, Package). **Behavioral** = dynamics over time: Use Case, Sequence (also Activity, State Machine, Communication).

questions.prompt: In a use case diagram, `<<include>>` vs `<<extend>>`:
options: include = MANDATORY (runs every time the base runs); extend = OPTIONAL (runs only when its condition applies, arrow points to the base)
Both are forms of actor generalization
include duplicates the use case text
questions.explain: **<<include>>**: the included use case MUST execute whenever the base executes (Transfer Funds → Verify OTP). **<<extend>>**: MAY extend under a condition (Convert Currency extends Transfer Funds for foreign currency); the arrow points FROM the extension TO the base. Actor generalization: Premium Customer inherits all Customer associations.

questions.prompt: Translating a UML class with `#amount`, an italic class name, and an `{abstract}` method `Process()` to C# gives:
options: public abstract class Payment { protected double amount; public abstract void Process(); }
public sealed class Payment { private double amount; public virtual void Process() {} }
public interface Payment { public double amount; void Process(); }
public static class Payment { internal double amount; static void Process(); }
questions.explain: UML → C# table: `#` = **protected**, `-` = private, `+` = public; italic/{abstract} = **abstract** class/method. Generalization = inheritance with base-constructor chaining (`: base(amount)`); a 1..* association becomes a collection field (`List<Payment> payments`).
